Corollary

/KOR-uh-lair-ee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Corollary means a natural or direct consequence that follows automatically from something else.

When the factory added a night shift, the corollary was a sudden demand for late-running buses.

Worked Example

A small island town finally got high-speed internet, and remote workers began moving in by the dozen. The newcomers brought welcome income to shops and cafes. But a corollary soon followed: with more people bidding on the same few houses, rents climbed beyond what many longtime residents could pay. No one had planned the rent spike; it flowed naturally from the arrival of the new workers.

The rent increase was not a separate accident; it followed naturally and automatically from the influx of new residents, which is exactly what a corollary is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

consequence: a result that follows from an action or condition

outgrowth: something that develops naturally out of something else

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cause: what makes something happen in the first place

precondition: something required before something else can happen

Where it sits · how necessarily the outcome follows — aftereffect → corollary → inevitability

aftereffect vs. corollary: An aftereffect is anything that lingers once an event is over, while a corollary follows logically and predictably from it.

inevitability vs. corollary: A corollary follows naturally from a first fact, but an inevitability is even stronger: an outcome that absolutely cannot be avoided.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — coroll

Root — coroll: from Latin corolla, a small garland or crown, diminutive of corona, crown

Suffix — -ary

Suffix — -ary: connected with, belonging to

Put it together

Put it together: Corollary comes from Latin corollarium, originally a tip or bonus paid in the form of a small garland (corolla, a little crown, from corona). Because the garland came as an extra on top of the main payment, corollary came to mean a truth or consequence you get automatically, like a bonus, once the first thing is established.

Use the root in a new word: coronation

Use the root in a new word: coronation: At a coronation the new monarch receives a crown, the Latin corona hiding inside corollary's own history as a little garland given as a bonus.

Word Choice

formal, academic register

Corollary usually appears as 'a corollary of' or 'a corollary to' a first fact or decision (a corollary of the new policy). It names what follows naturally and automatically once something else is true; it is not the cause of that thing, and not a result someone deliberately engineered.
